largely synchronous. In this short-form paper, we introduce bounded-staleness asynchronous ES and
demonstrate it on Endless Terminals benchmark using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Across three

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.04196v1 [cs.AI] 03 Oct 2026 \workshoptitle Transitioning from Pre-Training to Post-Training Asynchronous Is Nearly Free for Evolution Strategies on Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks William Hoy Affiliation: University of Miami Email: wjh58@miami.edu Jingxuan Fan Affiliation: Harvard University Email: jfan@g.harvard.edu Nurcin Celik Affiliation: University of Miami Email: celik@miami.edu Xu Pan Affiliation: Harvard University Email: xupan@fas.harvard.edu Abstract LLM-based long-horizon agentic post-training is often bottlenecked by rollout generation: trajectories span many interaction turns, completion times vary substantially, and synchronous update barriers leave faster workers waiting for stragglers. Asynchronous reinforcement learning which has been adopted in LLM post-training addresses this inefficiency by consuming trajectories as they arrive, but introduces policy lag and off-policy optimization. Evolution strategies (ES) offer a backpropagation-free alternative for LLM post-training, yet it relies on a larger number of rollouts and existing practices have remained largely synchronous. In this short-form paper, we introduce bounded-staleness asynchronous ES and demonstrate it on Endless Terminals benchmark using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Across three evaluation seeds, natural Async-1 matches synchronous ES, achieving 25.9% versus 25.4% held-out success. Controlled schedules that delay 10% of each update cohort by four or eight policy updates reduce success by only 1.6 and 3.1 percentage points, respectively, without explicit off-policy correction. GRPO performs better overall, reaching 29.0% held-out success, but importantly our results show that ES tolerates moderate policy staleness with limited degradation, opening possibilities for future improvement of ES-based post-training with asynchronous algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to demonstrate the effectiveness of sync and async ES on a multi-turn terminal style agentic coding task. 1 Introduction Post-training language agents increasingly requires long-horizon interactions with stateful environments. In these settings, trajectory lengths can vary substantially: short trajectories finish quickly, while long-running trajectories become stragglers. Synchronous training systems must wait for the slowest trajectories before performing an update, leaving faster workers idle and reducing hardware utilization ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Hou et al., 2026 ) . Asynchronous reinforcement learning addresses this straggler problem by consuming completed trajectories as they arrive rather than enforcing a strict rollout barrier ( Nair et al., 2015 ; Mnih et al., 2016 ; Espeholt et al., 2018 ) , which has been adopted to the LLM post-training ( Noukhovitch et al., 2024 ; Han et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ) . This improves worker utilization but introduces policy lag: some trajectories are generated by an older policy and consumed after the learner has already advanced. Such off-policy data can reduce training stability as the lag increases ( Hou et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Consequently, asynchronous training must balance higher utilization against the optimization error introduced by stale experience. Evolution strategies (ES) have recently emerged as a viable alternative to policy-gradient methods for LLM post-training ( Qiu et al., 2026 ; Hoy et al., 2026 ) (related works in Appendix G ). ES assigns credit at the trajectory level, avoids backpropagation through generated tokens, and requires only inference-level memory. Recent work has extended ES from single-turn reasoning tasks to long-horizon language agents ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . However, these studies use synchronous ES, retaining the same population-wide barrier that limits utilization on tasks with variable trajectory lengths. More concerningly, ES requires substantially more rollouts per update than policy-gradient methods. Each candidate policy must be evaluated on a cohort of tasks rather than a single task. Because these evaluations can vary considerably in completion time (Figure 2 ), synchronous ES must repeatedly wait for the slowest workers, creating particularly severe efficiency bottlenecks. Before adopting asynchronous ES for post-training, we must address a central question: how much policy staleness can ES tolerate before asynchronous evaluation begins to degrade learning? Unlike asynchronous policy-gradient methods, asynchronous ES consumes scalar fitness measurements of parameter perturbations evaluated around older central policies. It is therefore unclear whether stale perturbation evaluations remain useful after the central policy has advanced. We introduce a bounded-staleness asynchronous ES method (Figure 1 ) and apply it on Endless Terminals, a stateful, long-horizon terminal-agent benchmark. Our contributions are: 1. We develop an asynchronous ES coordinator that continuously dispatches perturbation evaluations, tracks their policy versions, and accepts results subject to a configurable maximum policy lag. 2. We compare synchronous ES with natural one-update asynchrony and controlled four- and eight-update delays. Natural Async-1 matches synchronous ES within the observed evaluation-seed variation. Relative to synchronous ES, controlled Async-4 and Async-8 reduce final held-out success by 1.6 and 3.1 percentage points, when accepted stale evaluations are used without modification. 3. To our knowledge, we present the first application of ES to LLM post-training on a stateful, multi-turn terminal-agent task. 2 Asynchronous ES Figure 1: Illustration of synchronous and natural asynchronous ES with G = 4 G=4 workers and update-cohort size N = 8 N=8 . Synchronous ES waits for the slowest perturbation before updating, leaving faster workers idle. Natural asynchronous ES updates after the eighth completed evaluation while unfinished perturbations remain in flight; those results return with a policy lag of one. We review the basics of ES and GRPO in the Appendix B and C . Synchronous ES evaluates all N N perturbations around the same central policy θ t \theta_{t} and waits for every fitness evaluation to finish before applying a step of update (Eq. 5 ). This population-wide barrier is expensive for long-horizon agentic tasks because trajectory durations vary substantially. Figure 2 characterizes the workload distribution of workers of a synchronous ES run under the same setup introduced in the following sections. The standard deviations of the workloads (i.e., time, number of generated tokens, and number of interaction turns) are in the same order as the mean. Near the end of an update, faster GPU workers may remain idle while the trainer waits for the slowest outstanding perturbation evaluations. Figure 2: Workload distribution for synchronous ES. Evaluation time is measured over all 3,600 perturbed policies from 120 updates. Solid and dashed lines denote the mean and median Our asynchronous ES implementation removes this population-wide barrier. Let G G denote the number of GPU workers and N N the ES update-cohort size. Each worker evaluates one perturbation at a time. In our experiments, each perturbation is evaluated on a batch of 256 multi-turn tasks, and its scalar reward is the mean binary success over that batch. Up to G G perturbation evaluations can remain in flight concurrently. Figure 1 illustrates how natural asynchronous dispatch eliminates the population barrier while allowing a bounded number of older-policy evaluations to remain in flight. Each completed evaluation returns its perturbation seed, from which perturbation ϵ i \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{i} is reconstructed, along with the reward R i R_{i} and the dispatch policy version v i v_{i} . Unlike synchronous ES, the reward may have been evaluated around an earlier central policy: R i = R ⁡ ( θ v i + σ ​ ϵ i ) . R_{i}=R\!\left(\theta_{v_{i}}+\sigma\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{i}\right). (1) Synchronous ES is the special case in which v i = t v_{i}=t for every member of the update cohort. If the current central-policy version is t t , we define the policy lag of a completed evaluation as ℓ i = t − v i . \ell_{i}=t-v_{i}. The result is accepted when ℓ i ≤ ℓ max , \ell_{i}\leq\ell_{\max}, where ℓ max \ell_{\max} is the maximum permitted policy staleness. Results that exceed this bound are logged, discarded, and replaced by subsequent completions. Once N N accepted results have accumulated, they form the update cohort. Reward standardization follows Eq. 4 and the central-policy update follows Eq. 5 , with μ R \mu_{R} and σ R \sigma_{R} computed over the N N accepted rewards rather than a synchronously evaluated population. An asynchronous update cohort may therefore contain perturbations evaluated around different recent versions of the central policy, but every accepted result satisfies the specified staleness bound. After a worker completes an evaluation, it first restores its unperturbed weights and replays any central-policy updates committed while it was busy. It then immediately begins a new perturbation from the current central policy. This allows faster workers to continue producing useful evaluations without waiting for slower workers. 3 Experimental Setup We initialized all methods from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and evaluated them on Endless Terminals Gandhi et al. (2026) , a stateful, multi-turn terminal benchmark with highly variable rollout lengths. We used 2,083 training tasks, 100 validation tasks, and 300 held-out test tasks. We compared scalar-reward GRPO (Appendix C ) with synchronous ES and three asynchronous ES variants: natural Async-1, controlled Async-4, and controlled Async-8. All methods used the same rollout and sampling configuration; complete hyperparameters are provided in Appendix D . Each ES update aggregated N = 30 N=30 perturbations, each evaluated on 256 tasks, and training ran for 120 updates. Synchronous ES waited for all 30 evaluations before beginning the next cohort. Under natural Async-1, each of the four workers began a new perturbation evaluation immediately after finishing its current one, and results with a policy lag of at most one update were accepted. Consequently, stale evaluations could constitute at most 3 / 30 = 10 % 3/30=10\% of an update cohort; the observed fraction was 9.5 % 9.5\% . To isolate the optimization effect of staleness from the utilization benefits of asynchronous execution, controlled Async-4 and Async-8 fixed the stale fraction at 10 % 10\% after warm-up. Each update combined 27 fresh evaluations with three evaluations delayed by exactly four or eight policy updates, respectively. GRPO baseline. Each GRPO step used 16 tasks with 16 rollouts per task, yielding 256 trajectories. The run completed one training epoch in 129 steps. Optimizer, regularization, and clipping configurations are reported in Appendix D . 4 Experimental Results Figure 3: Native-step training reward. All four ES schedules follow similar reward trajectories over 120 updates, indicating that controlled staleness up to lag 8 does not substantially alter the observed optimization path. GRPO reaches a higher training reward, although its batch-level rewards fluctuate more strongly between steps. ES iterations and GRPO steps represent different amounts of compute and should not be compared one-to-one. Figure 4: Mean held-out success across three stochastic evaluation seeds, with shaded regions showing sample standard deviation. Natural Async-1 closely tracks synchronous ES at the measured checkpoints.
